findings.title: Legacy SQL command path is not explicitly disabled
findings.body: UnmarshalSQLCommand is a separate entry point from ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery and does not check whether SQL expressions are disabled; it still calls NewSQLCommand. SQL is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList now fails when the stub DB returns 'not implemented', producing a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This defense-in-depth gap means restoring or replacing the stub DB implementation would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL path through this entry point without any explicit feature/security gate. Add the same explicit rejection here (and for direct NewSQLCommand/SQLCommand execution) rather than relying on the stubbed database to fail.

findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and can dereference a nil toggle source
findings.body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally, returns false when that value is true, and also returns false otherwise, so the feature-toggle check is dead logic that always disables SQL while obscuring the intent. It also dereferences h.features unconditionally for SQL queries; an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with a nil FeatureToggles (as test or auxiliary callers may do) will now panic instead of returning an error. Simplify this to an explicit unconditional return false (with a security comment) or handle a nil toggle source.

findings.title: No regression test covers disabling SQL expressions
findings.body: The PR changes the SQL query path to reject QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL database, but adds or updates no tests. There is no test proving that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor tests covering NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand and SQLCommand.Execute failing closed with the stubbed DB. Without these, a future refactor of the reader, command unmarshalling, or DB stub could accidentally re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 attack surface without CI noticing.
